---

### 3. Nature of Observations / Simulations Covered

* **Ensemble Means vs. Individual GCM Extrema:** The figures and reported values represent **multi-model ensemble averages** across five CMIP6 GCMs (CESM2, MRI-ESM2-0, BCC-CSM2-MR, GFDL-ESM4, and CanESM) [5, 6]. Individual GCM extrema are **not** reported separately for water footprint values in the text or figures [1, 2].
* **Period Averages vs. Annual Observations:** The data points reflect **multi-year period averages**—specifically the historical baseline period (1981–2014) and three 25–30 year future projection periods (2015–2039, 2040–2069, and 2070–2100) [5, 7]. They are **not** single-year annual observations or year-by-year simulated extremes [1, 5, 7].

references.cited_text: 3.3. WF changes under the CMIP6 climate scenarios The green WF was higher than the blue WF in the rainy season, while the blueWFwashighly consumed in the dry season. As a baseline, the total WFs of rice and maize production were between 1206 and 1467 and 682–866 m3 ton−1, respectively. Soybean, mung bean, and cassava had totalWFs of 542, 437, and 575m3 ton−1, respectively, com-pared to the baseline (Figs. 5–7). In irrigated areas, the total WF of rice production under the RRR cropping system continued to decline from near to far-future periods under the SSP245 scenario, while the total WF increased in mid and far-future periods under the SSP585 scenario. The highest greenWF occurred in the production of the first rice crop (758–1318 m3 ton−1, Fig. 5(a)), followed by the second (287–371 m3 ton−1, Fig. 5(b)) and third rice crops (153–194 m3 ton−1, Fig. 5(d)). The blue WF was highest in the third rice crop (803–1194 m3 ton−1, Fig. 5(d)), followed by the second (628–790 m3 ton−1, Fig. 5(b)) and first rice crops (55.4–95 m3 ton−1, Fig. 5(a)). The grey WF was 223–349 m3 ton−1, overall (Fig. 5(a), (b), and (c)).

In this study, five CMIP6 global circulation model datasets (CESM2, MRI-ESM2-0, BCC-CSM2-MR, GFDL-ESM4, and CanESM) were selected under three future periods: 2015–2039, 2040–2069, and 2070–2100. Furthermore, SSP245 (538.9 ppm CO2 equivalent) and SSP585 (936.4 ppm CO2 equivalent) were used to predict the major crop yield and WF changes in the future. This is because the SSP245 scenario is subjective to most countries striving for sustainable development, while the SSP585 scenario represents the worst scenario (energy-intensive, fossil-based economy), which embodies the impact of uncon-ventional development (O'Neill et al., 2016). The precipitation and maximumandminimum temperatures under CMIP6 climate projection were obtained from HAII, which were downscaled (at resolution 0.1 × 0.1° of grid size) and analyzed bias correction (Chaowiwat et al., 2016; Chaowiwat et al., 2019).

The multi-model ensemble average approach is widely used for cli-mate modelling to reduce the large biases and uncertainties from model parameterization errors, model structures, assumptions, and input variables (Khan et al., 2018; Ahmed et al., 2019). However, CMIP6 models have shown improvement based on the previous re-gional studies (e.g., Stouffer et al., 2017; Rivera and Arnould, 2020; Gusain et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021). Kim et al. (2020) reported that the CMIP6 models improve the limitation of the CMIP5 models in terms of the observed global and regional patterns of temperature ex-tremes. Bağçaci et al. (2021) indicated that CMIP6 models outperform CMIP5 models in terms of accuracy statistics, especially precipitation simulation. Meanwhile, the error in precipitation and temperature under CMIP6 models were reduced by 11% and 6%, respectively. Yazdandoost et al. (2021) revealed that CMIP6models showed less sys-tematic biases of precipitation simulation in the arid zone and underes-timation in the humid zone indicating high uncertainty in wet regions. Similar to in the Mainland South-East Asia (MSES), Iqbal et al. (2021) found that the CMIP6 models simulated the annual mean precipitation in the central and southern region of MSEA with a bias of less than 25%, whereas high biases (−25 to−75%) were detected in the western coastal region of Myanmar, where the highest precipitation was ob-served. However, CMIP6 models can be used for climate change projec-tions after correcting the related biases and uncertainties.

Climate data Historical climate data (1981–2014) were obtained from the Hydro and Agro Informatics Institute (Public Organization; HAII), which gath-ered data from the Thai Meteorological Department (TMD) at meteoro-logical stations in Phichit Province. The daily climate data were precipitation andmaximum andminimum temperatures. The daily rel-ative humidity, wind speed, andwinddirection during 1981–2014were collected from the Phichit Agromet station. These historical climate data were used as the baseline scenario.
